name: Xylazine
description: Xylazine (tranq) facts: why a veterinary sedative is in the fentanyl supply, effects, severe wounds, overdose response with naloxone, withdrawal, test strips, and federal scheduling.
quick: Xylazine is a veterinary sedative that has spread through the illicit fentanyl supply as "tranq". It is not approved for people. It deepens and prolongs sedation, is not reversed by naloxone, and causes severe skin wounds. It is not yet federally controlled, but the House passed a bill in September 2026 to place it in Schedule III, and many states already control it.
facts: Veterinary sedation only (horses, cattle, other animals)
Not federally controlled; House passed Schedule III bill (September 2026); controlled in many states
None for humans; give naloxone for the fentanyl

blocks.p: Xylazine is a sedative and muscle relaxant approved by the FDA only for animals. It is added to illicit fentanyl, probably to extend its effects cheaply. In 2023 the White House declared fentanyl mixed with xylazine an emerging threat.[[1]]
Most people who are exposed do not seek it out; it is mixed into the fentanyl supply, and buyers often do not know it is there.

sections.q: What are the effects of xylazine, and how long do they last?

blocks.p: Xylazine causes deep sedation, slow heart rate, low blood pressure, and slowed breathing. Combined with fentanyl, people may stay sedated for hours, which raises the risk of overdose, injury, assault, and pressure wounds.[[1]]

sections.q: What are the risks of xylazine?

blocks.p: **Severe wounds:** xylazine causes skin ulcers and dead tissue, often far from the injection site and even in people who smoke or snort it. Untreated wounds can lead to amputation. Early wound care helps.[[1]]
**Overdose:** combined with fentanyl, xylazine deepens sedation and slows breathing and heart rate. Naloxone reverses the fentanyl but not the xylazine.[[1]]
**Prolonged sedation** leaves people vulnerable to injury, hypothermia, and assault.

sections.q: How do you respond to a xylazine overdose?

blocks.p: A person may be deeply sedated, hard or impossible to wake, with slow breathing, a slow heartbeat, and low blood pressure. Because xylazine is almost always mixed with fentanyl, always give naloxone. Naloxone restores breathing from the fentanyl even if the person stays sleepy from the xylazine.[[1]][[2]]

emergency.title: If someone may have overdosed
items: Call 911 if the person is unresponsive, cannot be woken, has blue or gray lips, or is breathing slowly or not at all.
Give naloxone (Narcan or a generic nasal spray, sold without a prescription) into one nostril. If there is no response after 2 to 3 minutes, give another dose.
If you are trained, give rescue breaths. Otherwise place the person on their side so they do not choke.
Stay with them. Naloxone can wear off before xylazine does, so the overdose can return even after the person wakes up.
Most states have Good Samaritan laws that protect people who call 911 for an overdose from some drug charges.

blocks.p: Focus on breathing: if the person is breathing after naloxone but still sedated, place them on their side and stay with them. Do not give more naloxone just to wake them fully if they are breathing adequately. Xylazine test strips are available in many areas.

sections.q: Is xylazine addictive, and what is withdrawal like?

blocks.p: People exposed regularly to fentanyl with xylazine can develop xylazine withdrawal on top of opioid withdrawal. It can be severe and is not relieved by opioid medicines alone.[[1]]

timeline.title: Symptoms begin
timeline.text: Anxiety, irritability, restlessness, high blood pressure.

timeline.title: Peak
timeline.text: Severe agitation, dysphoria, fast heartbeat, high blood pressure.

blocks.p: Hospitals treat xylazine withdrawal with alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine, dexmedetomidine, or tizanidine, alongside buprenorphine or methadone for opioid withdrawal.

sections.q: Is xylazine legal in the US?

blocks.p: **Federal law:** xylazine is an FDA-approved veterinary drug and is not a federal controlled substance. The FDA restricted imports of xylazine ingredients in 2023 to keep it in legitimate veterinary channels.[[1]]

**Pending legislation:** the Combating Illicit Xylazine Act, which would place xylazine in Schedule III while protecting veterinary and agricultural use, passed the House unanimously in September 2026 and was awaiting Senate action.[[3]]

**State law:** many states, including Pennsylvania, Florida, Ohio, and West Virginia, have added xylazine to their controlled substance schedules. Selling it for human consumption can be prosecuted under several state and federal laws.

sections.q: Where can someone get help with xylazine use?

blocks.p: Xylazine wounds need medical care. Many syringe services programs and health centers offer wound care, test strips, and naloxone.

ul: **SAMHSA National Helpline:** 1-800-662-4357. Free, confidential, 24 hours a day, in English and Spanish. It gives referrals to local treatment and support.[[4]]
**FindTreatment.gov:** a federal locator for state-licensed treatment programs, searchable by location, payment, and type of care.[[5]]
**988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline:** call or text 988 for a mental health or substance use crisis.
**Your own clinician:** a primary care doctor can screen, treat, and refer, and can discuss medicines that support recovery where they exist.
